rv.q: Suh uses this real story as the armature for his instructive, occasionally devastating play.
The show is more anguished, more mournful, more urgent than before, and sometimes that makes it heavy-handed.

Bolstered by star-making performances from Shannon Tyo and Daniel K. Isaac, it is an intensely watchable, exquisite work of historical excavation centered around the first Chinese woman to set foot in the United States.

Suh keeps her alive as a witness to nearly two centuries of dark history, from the Opium Wars, and the Chinese Exclusion Act, and a series of incidents of brutal violence against Chinese-American laborers – and right up to the present moment.

Under the direction of Ma-Yi Theater Company's artistic director Ralph B. Peña, the production at The Public Theater is an evocative and eye-opening excavation of difference and a seductive appeal for greater understanding.
Afong Moy: human museum exhibition; emphasis on the "human." Afong Moy doesn't appear in history books. Records of her very existence stop after 1850, so she's too specialized to even be a Jeopardy!

Thanks to playwright Lloyd Suh and his elegant, illuminating The Chinese Lady —now at the Public Theater—we now have a glimpse into the life of Afong Moy, reportedly the first Chinese woman ever to set foot in America.
Ultimately, it is Tyo’s Moy who turns The Chinese Lady into a rich and challenging evening of theater.
Suh’s “The Chinese Lady” is one of those works, not unlike Bernard Pomerance’s “The Elephant Man” or Tim Burton’s “Ed Wood,” that bring light to a unique life as intriguing as it is disturbing.
But, yet again, it’s not really her story that she’s telling, and it makes for a less than fully fulfilling evening.

There are so many things to admire about Lloyd Suh's The Chinese Lady which is currently running at The Public Theater through April 10. And here are just a few of them. ADMIRATION #1: The Chinese Lady tells a fresh story.
The Chinese Lady directly challenges us to interrogate how we see.

Tyo has good chemistry with Isaac (who is on the TV show "Billions"), and they have a sibling relationship that is ultimately strained over time, giving us much-needed drama that the play, while informative and enjoyable, sorely lacks.
"'The Chinese Lady' charges toward its if-you-haven't-gotten-it-by-now-here's-the-message conclusion that seeks hope in a culture that is unforgiving and cruel.

cn.t: Critics find Lloyd Suh's play about the first Chinese woman in America a lyrical, illuminating exploration of exploitation and othering, though some find it grows tedious. Strong performances and sharp historical insights mostly overcome structural concerns.
